**A Thousand Words, Give or Take**

The instruction is simple: write a thousand words. No topic, no direction, no hidden rubric. Just a length, as if meaning could be portioned out like flour. I sit at my desk and watch the cursor blink, a small metronome counting silence. The room is quiet except for the hum of the refrigerator and the occasional car passing on the wet street below. It is morning, or maybe afternoon; time has a way of dissolving when the only task is to fill space with language.

I remember being in fourth grade when I first learned that words could be counted. My teacher, Mrs. Aldridge, assigned a five-hundred-word essay on the water cycle. I wrote four hundred and ninety-two and panicked. She told me the missing eight words didn't matter, but I couldn't stop thinking about them. Were they still out there somewhere, waiting to be used? Did they belong to me? That was the year I began to think of language as a finite resource, something you could run out of if you weren't careful.

But of course, language isn't like that. It replenishes itself. Every sentence I write creates the possibility of another. The constraint of a thousand words is artificial, but it has a strange power. It makes me aware of each word as a choice, each phrase as an expenditure. I find myself avoiding long words, then seeking them out, as if polysyllables could help me reach the target faster. That is the trap of word counts: they turn writing into arithmetic.

What would I say if I knew I had exactly one thousand words left? Not just for this exercise, but for my entire life? Would I hoard them, spending only the most necessary ones? Would I write a list of names, a sequence of I love yous, a final apology? The thought is melodramatic, but it persists. There is a long tradition of imagining the last words of the dying, the final entries in journals, the last transmissions from sinking ships. We are drawn to endings because they give shape to the middle. A thousand words is an ending in miniature.

The cursor continues to blink. I think about the first time I saw the ocean. I was seven, and my father drove us to the coast in a rented car that smelled of sunscreen and old coffee. I remember the way the horizon seemed to divide the world into two clean halves: blue above, blue below. I didn't have the words for it then. I said something like, "It's so big," and my father laughed and said, "Yes, it is." That was enough. Sometimes the simplest words are the truest.

Now I wonder if a thousand words could capture that moment. Probably not. The ocean resists description. Even the best writers—Melville, Woolf, Carson—only manage to gesture at its strangeness. The sea is always larger than the sentences we build around it. But perhaps that is the point of writing: not to contain the world, but to brush against it, to leave a mark that proves we were paying attention.

I pause to count what I have written. I am roughly three hundred words in. The number feels both too small and too large. Too small because I have not yet said what I meant to say; too large because I have already used so many words to say almost nothing. This is the paradox of writing. It is easy to fill a page with words, but difficult to fill them with meaning. The blank space between good sentences is where the real work happens.

Let me try to be more concrete. There is a mug of cold coffee on my desk. It is blue, with a chip on the rim. The coffee left a faint ring on the wood, a watermark shaped like an eclipse. I could write a paragraph about that ring. I could trace its circumference and imagine the cup that made it, the hand that held it, the morning light that fell across it. That would be a kind of truth, small but real. But it would also be a way of avoiding the larger truth: that I am writing about writing because I am afraid of what else might emerge if I stop controlling the flow.

Fear is a common companion to writing. Fear of being boring, fear of being wrong, fear of being seen too clearly. The word count, at least, gives me something to hide behind. As long as I am counting words, I don't have to count the ways in which I might fail. But failure is not the opposite of success; it is part of the process. Every writer fails, repeatedly. The only difference between a writer and a non-writer is that the writer keeps trying after the failure.

I think of Anne Lamott's advice about "shitty first drafts." She says that all good writing begins with terrible writing. The first draft is just about getting the words down, any words, in any order, so that you have something to shape later. This piece is a kind of first draft, though it may never be revised. It is a record of my mind at this particular moment, with all its hesitations and detours. Maybe that is enough.

What is a thousand words, really? It is about four pages of double-spaced text. It is the length of a short blog post, a brief letter, a miniature essay. It is long enough to develop a thought but short enough to require economy. It is a constraint that can be liberating, because it forces me to choose. And choice is the essence of art. The sculptor chooses which stone to remove; the painter chooses which color to lay down; the writer chooses which word to keep and which to cut.

I am now more than halfway through. The room has grown brighter; the sun has shifted from gray to pale gold. A bird is singing outside, a repetitive three-note call that sounds like a question. I don't know what kind of bird it is. If I had more words, I might try to describe it. But maybe not knowing is okay. Mystery is underrated in a world that demands explanations.

Here is a memory: I once found a box of letters in my grandmother's attic. They were tied with a faded blue ribbon, dozens of envelopes addressed in my grandfather's shaky hand. I opened one. It was a love letter, written during the war, full of longing and detail about the weather in some distant camp. The letter was exactly one page long, maybe two hundred words. It was enough. It told me more about love than any novel I had ever read.

It depends on what the words are doing, how they are arranged, whether they are true. I can write a thousand words about my mug of coffee, and if I do it with enough attention, it might become a meditation on mortality. Or I can write a thousand words about the meaning of life that remains abstract and hollow. The subject matters less than the seeing.

I have a friend who is a poet. She once told me that she spends weeks on a single line, trying to find the exact word. "The right word is a kind of magic," she said. "It opens a door in the reader's mind." I think about that as I write this quickly, without much revision. Am I using the right words? Probably not all of them. But there is also a magic in the quick, unguarded draft, the way it reveals the shape of a thought before it has been polished into smoothness.

So here I am, at the edge of my thousand words. The bird has stopped singing. The coffee is cold. The sun has moved across the floor. I have written about writing, about fear, about love letters and oceans and the water cycle. I have not said anything world-changing. But perhaps I have said something true. And that, I think, is what the instruction intended all along: not a thousand perfect words, but a thousand honest ones.

When the doctor told him he had exactly one thousand words left, Marcus laughed. It was a nervous laugh, two words maybe: "That's crazy." The doctor didn't smile. "It's a rare neurological condition," she said. "Your vocal cords will slowly calcify. You can speak, but each word accelerates the process. We estimate one thousand words before complete silence." That night, he lay awake and counted the words he had spoken that day. "Good morning" to the barista, two. "Thank you," two. "How are you" to his wife, three. "Fine," one. "Love you," two. He had spent words like pennies. Now he understood their value. He resolved to become a miser. He bought a small notebook and a pen. From now on, he would write everything. He would not speak unless absolutely necessary.

She smiled and kissed his cheek. At dinner, he pointed at the salt. She passed it. He wrote, "Good soup." She read it aloud. The silence was not yet heavy. It was a game, a novelty. Each unspoken word felt like money saved in an invisible bank. He kept a tally in the back of the notebook. Seven days. He had spent only thirty-one words. He had nine hundred and sixty-nine left.

I remember being in fourth grade when I first learned that words could be counted. My teacher, Mrs. Aldridge, assigned a five-hundred-word essay on the water cycle. I wrote four hundred and ninety-two and panicked. She told me the missing eight words didn't matter, but I couldn't stop thinking about them. Were they still out there somewhere, waiting to be used? Did they belong to me? That was the year I began to think of language as a finite resource, something you could run out of if you weren't careful.

But of course, language isn't like that. It replenishes itself. Every sentence I write creates the possibility of another. The constraint of a thousand words is artificial, but it has a strange power. It makes me aware of each word as a choice, each phrase as an expenditure. I find myself avoiding long words, then seeking them out, as if polysyllables could help me reach the target faster. That is the trap of word counts: they turn writing into arithmetic.

What would I say if I knew I had exactly one thousand words left? Not just for this exercise, but for my entire life? Would I hoard them, spending only the most necessary ones? Would I write a list of names, a sequence of I love yous, a final apology? The thought is melodramatic, but it persists. There is a long tradition of imagining the last words of the dying, the final entries in journals, the last transmissions from sinking ships. We are drawn to endings because they give shape to the middle. A thousand words is an ending in miniature.

The cursor continues to blink. I think about the first time I saw the ocean. I was seven, and my father drove us to the coast in a rented car that smelled of sunscreen and old coffee. I remember the way the horizon seemed to divide the world into two clean halves: blue above, blue below. I didn't have the words for it then. I said something like, "It's so big," and my father laughed and said, "Yes, it is." That was enough. Sometimes the simplest words are the truest.

Now I wonder if a thousand words could capture that moment. Probably not. The ocean resists description. Even the best writers—Melville, Woolf, Carson—only manage to gesture at its strangeness. The sea is always larger than the sentences we build around it. But perhaps that is the point of writing: not to contain the world, but to brush against it, to leave a mark that proves we were paying attention.

Too small because I have not yet said what I meant to say; too large because I have already used so many words to say almost nothing. This is the paradox of writing. It is easy to fill a page with words, but difficult to fill them with meaning. The blank space between good sentences is where the real work happens.

When the doctor told him he had exactly one thousand words left, Marcus laughed. It was a nervous laugh, two words maybe: "That's crazy." The doctor didn't smile. "It's a rare neurological condition," she said. "Your vocal cords will slowly calcify. You can speak, but each word accelerates the process. We estimate one thousand words before complete silence." Marcus sat in the cold examining room and did the math. One thousand words. He had already used four.

That night, he lay awake and counted the words he had spoken that day. "Good morning" to the barista, two. "Thank you," two. "How are you" to his wife, three. "Fine," one. "Love you," two. He had spent words like pennies. Now he understood their value. He resolved to become a miser. He bought a small notebook and a pen. From now on, he would write everything. He would not speak unless absolutely necessary.

The first week was an adventure. He communicated through gestures and notes. His wife, Elena, found it charming at first. He left a note on the bathroom mirror: "You look beautiful." She smiled and kissed his cheek. At dinner, he pointed at the salt. She passed it. He wrote, "Good soup." She read it aloud. The silence was not yet heavy. It was a game, a novelty. Each unspoken word felt like money saved in an invisible bank. He kept a tally in the back of the notebook. Seven days. He had spent only thirty-one words. He had nine hundred and sixty-nine left.

But the world is not built for silence. The phone rang. He stared at it. Elena said, "Aren't you going to answer?" He shook his head. She frowned. At work, his boss called him into an office and asked a direct question. Marcus wrote his answer on a sticky note. His boss looked at the note, then at him, then back at the note. "Are you okay?" Marcus nodded. The boss cleared his throat. "We need someone who can communicate verbally with clients." Marcus wrote: "I can still write." The boss said, "It's not the same." Marcus left the office without another word. He had saved three words, but lost his job.

At home, Elena was waiting. She had found the notebook. "What is this?" she asked, holding it up. The page was open to his tally. Marcus took a pen and wrote: "I have a condition. He imagined a future where he could not tell his daughter he loved her, could not shout her name at her graduation, could not speak at her wedding. He had a daughter, Sophie, twelve years old.
